issues.legal_issue: A prior decision rejecting an equality challenge to the special treatment of former rulers prevents the same challenge from being reopened.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the statutory requirement for Central Government consent before suing a ruler of a former Indian State.
A previous decision of the Supreme Court had rejected a challenge to the same provision under the equality guarantee.
The Court declined to reconsider the point and treated the prior decision as conclusive.
issues.conclusion: The equality challenge was no longer open for consideration.
issues.legal_principle: In Mohan Lal Jain v. His Highness Maharaja Shri Sawai Man Singhji, this Court had rejected the challenge under Article 14 to the special treatment afforded to former rulers. The Court applied that decision as conclusive of the equality issue.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_civil_suit_r: A litigant sought constitutional relief challenging a restriction on bringing a civil suit.
predicates.binding_prior_equality_ruling: A prior binding court decision had rejected an equality challenge to the same legal restriction.

issues.definition: When a litigant challenges a restriction on bringing a civil suit and a binding prior ruling has rejected the same equality challenge, the equality challenge is not reopened.

issues.legal_issue: The requirement of government consent before suing a former ruler was not an unreasonable restriction on the petitioners’ property rights in the historical circumstances underlying the provision.
material_facts: The petitioners sought to sue a former ruler over their claimed entitlement to maintenance as members of a joint Hindu family.
The petitioners alleged that the maintenance arrangement arose from a family custom and that either the former ruler or the Union was responsible for adequate maintenance.
The Central Government refused consent to the proposed suit.

The special treatment of former rulers arose from agreements and assurances connected with the integration of former Indian States, undertaken with the aim of bringing the country under one central government.
issues.conclusion: The consent requirement was not shown to impose an unreasonable restriction on the petitioners’ rights under Article 19(1)(f), and the provision was not invalid on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Article 19(1)(f), the Court held that the restriction imposed through sections 87B and 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure was reasonable in light of the historical and legislative background, including the agreements and assurances made to former rulers and the public interest in integrating the former States. The Court also relied on Mohan Lal Jain v. His Highness Maharaja Shri Sawai Man Singhji concerning the special treatment of former rulers. It observed that the historical basis for continuing the provision prospectively could weaken over time, but did not invalidate it in this case.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_civil_suit_r: A litigant challenged the constitutionality of a restriction on bringing a civil suit.
predicates.suit_targets_former_ruler: The proposed civil suit was against a ruler of a former State.
predicates.restriction_implements_historical_assura: The restriction continued protections associated with agreements or assurances made to former rulers.
predicates.restriction_serves_public_integration_pu: The protections were maintained as part of arrangements intended to bring former States under a central government.

issues.definition: If a constitutional challenge concerns a restriction on suing a former ruler that continues historical assurances and serves the integration purpose underlying those arrangements, the restriction is not unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: The authority deciding whether to permit a suit against a former ruler should ordinarily allow a genuine dispute that appears prima facie triable to be heard by a court.
material_facts: The petitioners sought consent to sue a former ruler over a claimed maintenance entitlement based on family custom.
The Court considered that the petitioners appeared prima facie to have a genuine grievance and that the dispute appeared triable by a court.
issues.conclusion: The authority should ordinarily grant consent for a genuine dispute that prima facie appears triable; refusal may be justified for frivolous claims. The Court left the petitioners’ particular grievance for the Central Government to consider and dismissed the writ petition without ordering that consent be granted.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court stated that the consent power should not be used to stifle claims. Consent should ordinarily, if not as a matter of course, be granted where a genuine dispute prima facie appears triable by a court; refusal may be justified where the claim is frivolous or clearly far-fetched.

predicates.sanction_application_for_suit_against_fo: A litigant sought prior consent to bring a civil suit against a former ruler.
predicates.genuine_dispute: The litigant presented a genuine dispute rather than a frivolous claim.
predicates.prima_facie_triable: The dispute appeared on its face to be one that a court could try.

issues.definition: When a litigant seeks consent to sue a former ruler over a genuine dispute that appears triable, consent should ordinarily be granted.
